question_en:
While organizing a display on the history of measurement, I found the glass object shown in the attachment. I need to check its identity and the history of the related length standards. Please answer the following questions:

1. What power-supply or discharge components can be seen at the top of the photo, inside the glass container, and at the side? Is this object a discharge light source or a laser? What is its name in the official collection record?
2. What standard did this object replace in the United States? In what years did its use as the US standard begin and end? What material was the replaced standard made from, and in what year did it become the US reference standard?
3. In which years did the later changes to the definition take place?

Answer format: Answer in numbered points (1)–(3). Each point should answer only its matching part and include all the information that part asks for.
answer:
(1) Top: two leads; inside the container: a long electrode or thin tube; side: a side branch tube and a separate thin tube on the left; type: discharge light source; official collection name: Krypton-86 Lamp (krypton-86 standard lamp).

(2) Replaced standard: National Prototype Meter Bar No. 27; years the lamp was used as the US standard: 1960–1983; material of the replaced meter bar: platinum–10% iridium alloy; year it became the US reference standard: 1893.

(3) 1983 and 2018.
gold_trajectory:
# Detailed Simulated Search Trajectory · P2-8-2-E02

## Step 01 · First record the visible structure of the glass object

Action: Examine the top, the interior of the container, and the side separately; do not directly call it a laser just because it involves the definition of the metre. Example query: NIST museum krypton 86 lamp glass electrodes metre standard.

Evidence observation: Two leads at the top, a long electrode/thin tube inside the container, and a side branch tube plus a separate thin tube on the left constitute search clues for a gas-discharge object. The photo provides structural observation, but the precise instrument name still requires collection records.

Evidence links:
https://www.nist.gov/image/krypton-86-lamp
https://www.nist.gov/sites/default/files/images/2023/10/04/1998.0543.001A_02-Krypton-86%20Lamp.jpg

Result of this step: Take discharge light source as the candidate and search for the same NIST photo.

## Step 02 · Confirm the instrument name by comparing with the original NIST collection image

Action: Open the official image page for the Krypton-86 Lamp and match the glass container, leads, and side tubes to the input subject.

Evidence observation: The official title is Krypton-86 Lamp, with image credit to the NIST Museum Collection; the original image file is named 1998.0543.001A_02-Krypton-86 Lamp. Do not treat the file number or the webpage update date as the years the instrument was used as a standard.

Evidence links:
https://www.nist.gov/image/krypton-86-lamp
https://www.nist.gov/sites/default/files/images/2023/10/04/1998.0543.001A_02-Krypton-86%20Lamp.jpg

Result of this step: The formal name for Question 1 is determined.

## Step 03 · Distinguish between lamp and laser using luminescence mechanism data

Action: Read the collection page's description of electrically excited atoms, and consult related implementation materials from the 1960 CGPM.

Evidence observation: NIST text describes it as electrically excited Krypton-86 atoms emitting light of a specific wavelength, consistent with a discharge light source; BIPM materials discuss the discharge lamp implementation of the standard radiation. Later advances in laser metrology represent another historical stage and do not change the fact that this object is a krypton-86 lamp.

Evidence links:
https://www.nist.gov/image/krypton-86-lamp
https://www.bipm.org/en/-/resolution-cgpm-11-7

Result of this step: Fill in the type as discharge light source, not laser.

## Step 04 · Read from the krypton lamp record what object it replaced

Action: Locate the sentence on the collection page stating when it replaced which US standard, preserving No. 27 in full.

Evidence observation: The page records that this lamp replaced National Prototype Meter Bar No. 27 as the US primary length standard in 1960, and the interval during which the metre was defined by the radiation wavelength of krypton-86 was 1960–1983. This is merely the handover of specific physical standards in the US and should not be conflated with the entire set of international prototypes.

Evidence links:
https://www.nist.gov/image/krypton-86-lamp

Result of this step: Obtain the replaced object and the usage interval of the krypton lamp for Question 2.

## Step 05 · Independently search for Meter Bar 27 rather than guessing the material from the name

Action: Example query: site:nist.gov "Meter Bar 27" platinum iridium 1893. Open an independent collection page to verify the material and photo.

Evidence observation: The NIST record for Meter Bar 27 gives platinum–10% iridium alloy; the No. 27 designation corresponds to the US National Prototype Metre. Do not infer the alloy from the metal color, and do not write 10% as the proportion of platinum.

Evidence links:
https://www.nist.gov/image/meter-bar-27
https://www.nist.gov/sites/default/files/styles/social/public/images/2016/09/22/meter27.jpg?itok=XbaJAtWQ

Result of this step: Fix the material as platinum–10% iridium.

## Step 06 · Verify the starting year of the US reference standard

Action: In the main text for Meter Bar 27, check the years of the Mendenhall Order and the Coast and Geodetic Survey Report.

Evidence observation: The record states that after the 1893 Mendenhall Order, No. 27 became the reference standard for all length measurements in the US and remained so until 1960. The 1889 node in BIPM history is the definition point for the international prototype, which is different from the 1893 node for the US reference standard.

Evidence links:
https://www.nist.gov/image/meter-bar-27
https://www.bipm.org/en/history-si/metre

Result of this step: Adopt 1893 as the starting year for Question 2.

## Step 07 · Establish the historical connection from the physical metre bar to atomic radiation

Action: Read the BIPM metre history page and the 1960 Resolution 6 to confirm the definition applicable to the stage of this lamp.

Evidence observation: The 1960 definition used the radiation wavelength in vacuum of a specific transition of Kr-86; Resolution 6 gives 1,650,763.73 wavelengths. This explains why the krypton lamp could replace the physical metre bar. This complete definition is background for search verification; the current question does not require reciting the numerical value.

Evidence links:
https://www.bipm.org/en/history-si/metre
https://www.bipm.org/en/committees/cg/cgpm/11-1960/resolution-6

Result of this step: 1960 is the starting point of the krypton lamp stage; subsequent steps need to find the year of the definition that replaced it.

## Step 08 · Check the implementation conditions of the 1960 standard radiation as corroborating evidence for the type

Action: Read Resolution 7 and its attached implementation notes, distinguishing between the implementation requirements for the discharge lamp and the definitional text for the unit of metre.

Evidence observation: Archived materials mention implementation conditions such as a hot-cathode discharge lamp and approximately 64 K; these materials are used to confirm the object is a specific atomic radiation light source, but they are insufficient to determine from the photo whether it was operating under those conditions at the time. The question does not require temperature, purity, or capillary parameters.

Evidence links:
https://www.bipm.org/en/-/resolution-cgpm-11-7
https://www.bipm.org/en/committees/cg/cgpm/11-1960/resolution-6

Result of this step: Retain only the type verification; do not add extra experimental operations to the final answer.

## Step 09 · Trace the original resolution for the 1983 definition change

Action: Enter the 17th CGPM Resolution 1 and check the Definition of the metre and the statement abolishing the old definition.

Evidence observation: The 1983 resolution adopted the definition of the metre as the length of the path travelled by light in vacuum during a time interval of 1/299792458 of a second, and explicitly abolished the 1960 Kr-86 definition. This also aligns with the NIST krypton lamp standard interval endpoint of 1983.

Evidence links:
https://www.bipm.org/en/committees/cg/cgpm/17-1983/resolution-1
https://www.bipm.org/en/history-si/metre
https://www.nist.gov/image/krypton-86-lamp

Result of this step: The first year for Question 3 is 1983.

## Step 10 · Trace the 2018 fixed constant system formulation

Action: Enter the 26th CGPM Resolution 1 and, combined with the BIPM history page, distinguish between the resolution year and the effective date.

Evidence observation: The 2018 resolution uses the fixed constant system to explain the dependence of the metre on the fixed speed of light c, and it became effective on 2019-05-20. The question asks for the year the definition change occurred; adopt the resolution year 2018, and do not substitute the effective year 2019.

Evidence links:
https://www.bipm.org/en/committees/cg/cgpm/26-2018/resolution-1
https://www.bipm.org/en/history-si/metre

Result of this step: The second year for Question 3 is 2018.

## Step 11 · Arrange the timeline by event type

Action: Separately review the three levels: international definition, US physical reference, and specific lamp usage.

Evidence observation: The US No. 27 reference standard started in 1893; the krypton lamp replaced it in 1960 and served as the US standard until 1983; subsequent definition changes occurred in 1983 and 2018. The 1889 international prototype node and the 2019 effective date can explain the background, but neither occupies the three time slots asked for in the question.

Evidence links:
https://www.nist.gov/image/krypton-86-lamp
https://www.nist.gov/image/meter-bar-27
https://www.bipm.org/en/history-si/metre

Result of this step: Avoid misplacing different dates within the same historical narrative.

## Step 12 · Re-check whether the object structure matches the formal terminology

Action: Compare the three structural observations from Question 1 again with the original NIST image, and then check whether the final answer includes any extraneous definitional details.

Evidence observation: Two leads, a long electrode/thin tube inside, a side branch tube, and a separate thin tube are the structures shown in the image; Krypton-86 Lamp is the collection name; discharge light source is the type derived from combining the image with the official mechanism description. The record does not require a laser cavity, additional devices, or complete technical parameters; none of these are fabricated.

Evidence links:
https://www.nist.gov/sites/default/files/images/2023/10/04/1998.0543.001A_02-Krypton-86%20Lamp.jpg
https://www.nist.gov/image/krypton-86-lamp

Result of this step: Answer the three sub-questions separately according to structure/standard handover/subsequent years.

## Step 13 · Verify question requirements and output scope

Action: Correspond each publicly required item one-by-one with the evidence above, checking the total count, positive/negative items, and field format.

Evidence observation: Retain the name, visible structure, 1960–1983, No. 27, platinum–10% iridium, 1893, and 1983/2018; supplementary resolutions and photo links can be reviewed in the trajectory, but the final answer does not add constant formulas not asked for in the question.

Result of this step: Write only the requested information into the final answer; keep the search process and exclusion criteria in the trajectory.

## Step 14 · Final Answer

(1) Top: two leads; inside the container: a long electrode or thin tube; side: a side branch tube and a separate thin tube on the left; type: discharge light source; official collection name: Krypton-86 Lamp (Krypton-86 Standard Lamp).

(2) Replaced standard: National Prototype Meter Bar No. 27; years the lamp was used as the US standard: 1960–1983; material of the replaced meter bar: platinum–10% iridium alloy; year it became the US reference standard: 1893.

(3) 1983 and 2018.
